2. Literature Review
2.1 Translationese in Human Speech-to-Text Translation
The concept of translationese — distinctive linguistic features that mark
translated text as different from originally authored content — has been a
central focus in Translation Studies for decades. Martin Gellerstam (1986)
first coined the term to describe the fingerprints that source languages leave on target texts
identifying lexical and syntactic patterns that distinguish Swedish
translations from original Swedish texts. This pioneering work established
that translations constitute a distinct textual category with identifiable
linguistic characteristics. Mona Baker (1993) expanded this concept by
proposing translation universals — features that appear in translated texts
regardless of language pairs involved. These include simplification (reduced
lexical diversity)
normalization (conforming to target language conventions)
(convergence toward the middle of the continuum of any linguistic feature).
Baker's framework has been instrumental in shifting translation research
toward corpus-based methodologies that can empirically identify these
patterns.
Subsequent advances in both statistical and neural machine translation have
added new dimensions to translationese research. Antonio Toral and Andrew
Way (2018) showed that machine translations exhibit their own distinctive
patterns of translationese
column2: often amplifying certain features found in human

column1: translations. Their analysis of WMT (Workshop on Machine Translation)
evaluation campaigns revealed that machine translation processes tend to
produce outputs with lower lexical variety and higher source language
interference than human translations. Recent work by  reframes translationese as a distinct
language within multilingual NMT models. Their
research demonstrates that biasing models to produce translationese outputs
inflates BLEU scores while decreasing human-rated quality — a finding that
underlines the divergence between automated metrics and genuine translation
quality. This reconceptualization of translationese as a computational
property rather than merely a linguistic artifact represents an important
theoretical advancement.
